newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian ruler wins some accolades for reforms.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian ruler wins some accolades for reforms.

text.p: Although reviled for human rights abuses and lack of democracy in Nigeria, military ruler General Sani Abacha nevertheless seems to be winning some accolades for the gradual reform of his chaotic nation.

Abacha, who seized power three years ago, capped two years of hard-nosed economic reforms on Wednesday by inaugurating a large team to plan how Nigeria can be turned into a developed nation under a programme tagged "Vision 2010".

Membership of the committee cuts across a wide spectrum of society and includes foreigners playing a key role in Nigeria's economy such as the chief executives of the oil-producing firms, giving it some credibility among the business community.
"Vision 2010 is another coup for Abacha," said banker Kunle Thomas. "At least on paper it means well and shows how seriously the regime has taken the burden of turning the economy round."
Arthur Mbanefo, one of Nigeria's top accountants and a member of the 172-strong committee, said the programme would consider how best to solve every single issue of the Nigerian crisis.
"We are going to look at everything, the educational system, crime, agriculture...everything," he told state television.

Abacha has faced a series of problems since taking power and confronted them head-on at nearly every turn but management of the economy has been where most commentators, foreigners and Nigerians alike, agree definite progress has been made.

After a doubtful start in 1994 when he fixed exchange and interest rates, Abacha made a dramatic u-turn the following year when he legalised the autonomous foreign exchange market where the naira is freely traded.
Fuel prices were raised four-fold attacking in one blow the long-postponed issue of low pump prices that encouraged smuggling to neighbouring countries of cheap Nigerian fuel.

In 1995 fiscal budget discipline resulted in a surplus, albeit a small one, for the first time in many years and finally tamed runaway annual inflation, down to 24.6 percent by last month compared with around 80 percent in December 1995.
Sanity has been restored in a banking system where nearly half of Nigerian financial institutions were in distress in 1994 because of blatant stealing by executives and dubious lending.

Scores of bankers and businessmen, many of them hitherto untouchable personalities are now behind bars, having been found guilty by failed banks tribunals set up to recover the loot and punish fraudulent people.
"The combination of these measures has put the economy in shape and with proper follow-up we should begin to see some significant growth soon," said industrialist Hassan Musa.
A World Bank report in preparation which has been widely reported in the Nigerian press forecasts that the non-oil sector of the economy could in fact grow by up to 7.5 percent.
"If reforms of 1995-96 are sustained and others quickly put in place, Nigeria can grow the non-oil economy at 7.5 percent per year, reduce poverty, and protect the environment,' it said.
Abacha envisages that Vision 2010 would provide a master plan for sustained development of Nigeria with annual gross domestic product growth rate of between six and 10 percent.
But while the economy may be coming right for the first time in many years, political stability remains tenuous for Nigeria.
Moshood Abiola, presumed winner of an annulled 1993 presidential election, has been in detention since 1994 when he defied Abacha and proclaimed himself president.
Some of his supporters are also in detention while many others have long fled abroad where they wage a campaign against Abacha's government that deters potential investors.

Nigeria's previously warm ties with Western nations are on ice over the slow pace of democratisation and human rights issues, most notably last year's hanging of nine minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa on murder charges.
Abacha' critics argue that Vision 2010 is a signal that he will be in power long after 1998 when he has promised he would hand over to a democratically elected president.
"Vision 2010 is evidence of the regime's determination at self-perpetuation," said Sylvester Odion-Akhaine, general secretary of the Campaign for Democracy pressure group.
Government officials deny this, saying 2010 was chosen since it will mark 50 years of Nigeria's independence from Britain.
